claim: Neurotransmitter release is mediated by the fast, calcium-triggered fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic plasma membrane.
source: Neurotransmitter release is mediated by the fast, calcium-triggered fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic plasma membrane, followed by endocytosis and recycling of the membrane of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: After exocytosis, synaptic vesicle membrane components are retrieved mainly by clathrin-dependent endocytosis.
source: After exocytosis, the components of the synaptic vesicle membrane are retrieved, mainly by clathrin-dependent endocytosis, and then used to regenerate synaptic vesicles for another round of exo-endocytotic recycling (Sudhof, 2013; Rizzoli, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sudhof, 2013 and Rizzoli, 2014.

claim: The study identified 252 phosphosites that are either up- or downregulated upon triggering calcium-dependent exocytosis.
source: Using rigorous quantification, we identified 252 phosphosites that are either up- or downregulated upon triggering calcium-dependent exocytosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulated changes of phosphosites within protein constituents of the presynaptic active zone, including bassoon, piccolo, and RIM1, were particularly pronounced.
source: Particularly pronounced were regulated changes of phosphosites within protein constituents of the presynaptic active zone, including bassoon, piccolo, and RIM1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only a small proportion of synaptic vesicles participate in recycling under normal physiological conditions.
source: Furthermore, functionally distinct pools of synaptic vesicles coexist in each nerve terminal, with only a small proportion of them participating in recycling under normal physiological conditions (Denker et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Denker et al., 2011.

claim: Synapsin1 was the first presynaptic protein to be discovered because it undergoes rapid phosphorylation upon depolarization of the presynaptic nerve terminal.
source: In fact, synapsin1 was the first presynaptic protein to be discovered because it undergoes rapid phosphorylation upon depolarization of the presynaptic nerve terminal (Ueda et al., 1981; Dolphin and Greengard, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ueda et al., 1981 and Dolphin and Greengard, 1981.

claim: Dynamin is rapidly dephosphorylated by a calcium-dependent phosphatase (calcineurin).
source: Additionally, the key protein in membrane fission, dynamin, is rapidly dephosphorylated by a calcium-dependent phosphatase (calcineurin) (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 1994.

claim: Dephosphorylation of dynamin alters its affinity for some of its binding partners involved in endocytosis.
source: Dephosphorylation alters the affinity of dynamin for some of its binding partners involved in endocytosis (Robinson et al., 1994; Anggono et al., 2006; Clayton and Cousin, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Robinson et al., 1994; Anggono et al., 2006; Clayton and Cousin, 2009.

claim: Several proteins involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis, termed 'dephosphins', are dephosphorylated upon depolarization in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: In addition to dynamin, several other proteins involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis, termed 'dephosphins' are dephosphorylated upon depolarization, in calcium-dependent manner, including the scaffold proteins amphiphysin1 and amphiphysin2, the PtdIns(4,5)P phosphatase synaptojanin, the adapter proteins epsin, eps15, and AP180 (Cousin and Robinson, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cousin and Robinson, 2001.

claim: Phosphorylation of SNAP-25 at Ser187 accelerates vesicle recruitment.
source: For example, phosphorylation of the SNARE SNAP-25 at Ser187 accelerates vesicle recruitment (Nagy et al., 2002), regulates formation of SNARE complex (Gao et al., 2016) and consequently promotes exocytosis in PC12 cells, and it is also induced by stress in affected brain regions (Yamamori et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagy et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2016; Yamamori et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of SNAP-25 at Thr138 interferes with assembly of SNARE complex and exocytosis.
source: Additionally, it was reported that phosphorylation of SNAP-25 at Thr138 interferes with assembly of SNARE complex and exocytosis (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2016.

claim: Phosphorylation of syntaxin1 at Ser14 and Ser188 regulates its interaction with Munc18-1.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of syntaxin1 at Ser14 and Ser188 regulates its interaction with Munc18-1 (Tian et al., 2003; Rickman and Duncan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tian et al., 2003; Rickman and Duncan, 2010.

claim: Dephosphorylation of NSF at Tyr83 and Thr645 promotes secretory vesicle fusion.
source: Dephosphorylation of N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor (NSF) at Tyr 83 and Thr645 was reported to promote secretory vesicle fusion (Huynh et al., 2004), probably by enhancing disassembly of SNARE complexes (Belluzzi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huynh et al., 2004 and Belluzzi et al., 2016.

claim: Synapsin1 is phosphorylated at Ser9 by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I (CaMKI).
source: For example, synapsin1 is phosphorylated at Ser9 by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I (CaMKI).
evidence: This is established knowledge about synapsin1 phosphorylation.

claim: Synapsin1 is phosphorylated by CaMKII at its C terminus (Ser566 and 603).
source: It is also phosphorylated by mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and CdK5 at both N and C termini (Ser62, Ser67, Ser549 and Ser551) and by CaMKII at its C terminus (Ser566 and 603) (Cesca et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cesca et al., 2010.

claim: The tyrosine-kinase Src phosphorylates synapsin1 at Tyr301.
source: Moreover, the tyrosine-kinase Src phosphorylates synapsin1 at Tyr301 (Onofri et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Onofri et al., 2007.

claim: Phosphorylation of synapsin1 at Ser9, Ser566 and Ser603 upon stimulation decreases actin binding and increases exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: While phosphorylation of Ser9, Ser566 and Ser603 upon stimulation decreases actin binding and increases exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, phosphorylation of Tyr301 has the opposite effect (Cesca et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cesca et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation of synapsin1 at Tyr301 has the opposite effect to phosphorylation at Ser9, Ser566 and Ser603.
source: While phosphorylation of Ser9, Ser566 and Ser603 upon stimulation decreases actin binding and increases exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, phosphorylation of Tyr301 has the opposite effect (Cesca et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cesca et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation of synapsin1 at Ser62, Ser67, Ser549 and Ser551 is downregulated upon stimulation of neurotransmitter release.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation at Ser62, Ser67, Ser549 and Ser551 is downregulated upon stimulation of neurotransmitter release and decreases the binding of synapsin to actin filaments, leading to the suggestion that phosphorylation by Cdk5 at Ser549 and 551 defines the ratio between resting and recycling synaptic vesicle pools (Verstegen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verstegen et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation by Cdk5 at Ser549 and 551 of synapsin1 defines the ratio between resting and recycling synaptic vesicle pools.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation at Ser62, Ser67, Ser549 and Ser551 is downregulated upon stimulation of neurotransmitter release and decreases the binding of synapsin to actin filaments, leading to the suggestion that phosphorylation by Cdk5 at Ser549 and 551 defines the ratio between resting and recycling synaptic vesicle pools (Verstegen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verstegen et al., 2014.

claim: Syntaxin1A, synaptobrevin (VAMP) and SNAP25 are phosphorylated by calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII).
source: Based on this classical approach, we know that for example syntaxin1A, synaptobrevin (VAMP) and SNAP25 are phosphorylated by calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII); synaptobrevin and SNAP25 by protein kinase C (PKC), and synaptotagmin1 and syntaxin1A by casein kinase II (CK2) (Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996.

claim: Synaptobrevin and SNAP25 are phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC).
source: Based on this classical approach, we know that for example syntaxin1A, synaptobrevin (VAMP) and SNAP25 are phosphorylated by calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII); synaptobrevin and SNAP25 by protein kinase C (PKC), and synaptotagmin1 and syntaxin1A by casein kinase II (CK2) (Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996.

claim: Synaptotagmin1 and syntaxin1A are phosphorylated by casein kinase II (CK2).
source: Based on this classical approach, we know that for example syntaxin1A, synaptobrevin (VAMP) and SNAP25 are phosphorylated by calcium/calmodulin dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII); synaptobrevin and SNAP25 by protein kinase C (PKC), and synaptotagmin1 and syntaxin1A by casein kinase II (CK2) (Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 1993; Nielander et al., 1995; Hirling and Scheller, 1996; Shimazaki et al., 1996.

claim: The study identified 4961 proteins in the synaptosome proteome.
source: We identified 4961 proteins (for list of identified proteins see Supplementary file 1, available at Dryad [Kohansal-Nodehi et al., 2016]) in the proteome and 1257 phosphoproteins in the phosphoproteome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study identified 1257 phosphoproteins in the synaptosome phosphoproteome.
source: We identified 4961 proteins (for list of identified proteins see Supplementary file 1, available at Dryad [Kohansal-Nodehi et al., 2016]) in the proteome and 1257 phosphoproteins in the phosphoproteome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most functions related to neurotransmission and synaptic vesicle recycling are enriched in both proteome and phosphoproteome datasets.
source: The analysis revealed that most of the functions related to neurotransmission and synaptic vesicle recycling are enriched in both proteomes, with a higher enrichment being observed in the phosphoproteome compared to the proteome (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher enrichment of neurotransmission and synaptic vesicle recycling functions is observed in the phosphoproteome compared to the proteome.
source: The analysis revealed that most of the functions related to neurotransmission and synaptic vesicle recycling are enriched in both proteomes, with a higher enrichment being observed in the phosphoproteome compared to the proteome (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phosphorylation events occur predominantly, and perhaps exclusively, inside the presynaptic nerve terminal under the experimental conditions.
source: However, it documents that even though synaptosomes are contaminated with many other organelles and post synaptic density proteins, the phosphorylation events occur predominantly, and perhaps exclusively, inside the presynaptic nerve terminal under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment analysis of the data.

claim: Only a small fraction (12–15%) of all quantified phosphosites show significant changes upon depolarization in the presence of Ca2+.
source: First, only a small fraction (12–15% ) of all quantified phosphosites show significant changes upon depolarization in the presence of Ca2+ (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Both phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events are detectable upon depolarization in the presence of Ca2+, with phosphorylation events being slightly more prominent.
source: Both phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events are detectable, with phosphorylation events being slightly more prominent (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The overlap among all quantified phosphosites is very high between the two comparisons (K+, Ca2+ versus K+, EGTA and K+, Ca2+ versus EGTA).
source: The overlap among all quantified phosphosites is very high between the two comparisons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is substantial overlap in regulated phosphosites between the two comparisons (37% in upregulated and 35% in downregulated phosphosites).
source: There is also substantial overlap in regulated phosphosites between the comparisons (37% in upregulated and 35% in downregulated phosphosites, Figure 2E–G) with identical tendency of regulation and similar fold changes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Only a limited set of proteins undergo rapid phosphorylation changes that are specifically triggered by Ca2+.
source: Taken together, these data show that only a limited set of proteins undergo rapid phosphorylation changes that are specifically triggered by Ca2+, most probably involving Ca2+-dependent kinases and phosphatases (see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Under stimulation conditions, synapsin1 (Ser603) was identified as an upregulated phosphosite.
source: As expected, under stimulation conditions, synapsin1 (Ser603) and dynamin1 (Ser774) (Figure 1A) were identified as up- and downregulated phosphosites, respectively (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Under stimulation conditions, dynamin1 (Ser774) was identified as a downregulated phosphosite.
source: As expected, under stimulation conditions, synapsin1 (Ser603) and dynamin1 (Ser774) (Figure 1A) were identified as up- and downregulated phosphosites, respectively (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Addition of KCl led to a fast increase in glutamate release that persisted for several minutes after depolarization.
source: As expected, addition of KCl led to a fast increase in glutamate release that persisted for several minutes after depolarization and that was reduced in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the glutamate release assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Glutamate release upon KCl addition was reduced in the absence of Ca2+.
source: As expected, addition of KCl led to a fast increase in glutamate release that persisted for several minutes after depolarization and that was reduced in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the glutamate release assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The difference between glutamate release in the presence and absence of calcium represents exocytotic release.
source: It has been shown that the difference between glutamate release in the presence and absence of calcium represents exocytotic release whereas the increase upon depolarization in the absence of Ca2+ is due to non-exocytotic release caused by the reversal of glutamate transporters in the plasma membrane that depend on the membrane potential (Nicholls and Sirha, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholls and Sirha, 1986.

claim: The increase in glutamate upon depolarization in the absence of Ca2+ is due to non-exocytotic release caused by the reversal of glutamate transporters in the plasma membrane.
source: It has been shown that the difference between glutamate release in the presence and absence of calcium represents exocytotic release whereas the increase upon depolarization in the absence of Ca2+ is due to non-exocytotic release caused by the reversal of glutamate transporters in the plasma membrane that depend on the membrane potential (Nicholls and Sirha, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholls and Sirha, 1986.

claim: Synapsin1 (Ser603) and dynamin1 (Ser774) are regulated antagonistically by Ca2+-influx, with synapsin being phosphorylated and dynamin being dephosphorylated.
source: These two sites are known to be regulated antagonistically by Ca2+-influx, with synapsin being phosphorylated and dynamin being dephosphorylated (Jovanovic et al., 2001; Graham et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jovanovic et al., 2001 and Graham et al., 2007.

claim: Both synapsin1 (Ser603) and dynamin1 (Ser774) changed their phosphorylation status as expected upon stimulation.
source: As shown in Figure 1B and C, both sites changed their phosphorylation status as expected, confirming that the synaptosomes are functional.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Proteins undergoing phosphorylation changes during Ca2+-dependent stimulation are all involved in synaptic vesicle trafficking or in presynaptic signaling.
source: With only a few exceptions (e.g. translation/transcription or neurotransmitter metabolism related proteins), proteins undergoing phosphorylation changes during Ca2+-dependent stimulation are all involved in synaptic vesicle trafficking or in presynaptic signaling (Figure 3A and B), again documenting the specificity of the experimental approach.
evidence: This is a finding from the functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Postsynaptic proteins, particularly proteins associated with the post synaptic density, were largely missing from the regulated phosphoproteins.
source: Note that postsynaptic proteins, particularly proteins associated with the post synaptic density, were largely missing (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Some proteins (e.g. bassoon, RIM1, synapsin1, dynamin1) contain multiple phosphorylation sites that can undergo parallel phosphorylation and dephosphorylations.
source: In addition, it is evident that some of the proteins (e.g. bassoon, RIM1, synapsin1, dynamin1) contain multiple phosphorylation sites that can undergo parallel phosphorylation and dephosphorylations.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Proteins of the active zone were most heavily phosphorylated.
source: Surprisingly, proteins of the active zone were most heavily phosphorylated, which is discussed further below.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most of the phosphosites in the Clathrin-Mediated Endocytosis (CME) functional group were dephosphorylated upon stimulation in the presence of Ca2+.
source: With few exceptions, most of the phosphosites in the Clathrin-Mediated Endocytosis (CME) functional group were dephosphorylated upon stimulation in the presence of Ca2+ (13 out of 15 regulated phosphosites in the depolarization with Ca2+ versus depolarization without Ca2+ comparison and 12 out 17 in the depolarization with Ca2+ versus no depolarization comparison) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Phosphorylation of the adaptor protein AP180 weakens its interaction with the AP-2 adaptor complex, which is required for synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
source: For example, phosphorylation of the adaptor protein AP180 weakens its interaction with the AP-2 adaptor complex, which is required for synaptic vesicle endocytosis (Hao et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hao et al., 1999.

claim: Three AP180 phosphosites (Ser600, Ser621 and Ser627) are dephosphorylated upon stimulation.
source: In our dataset, three AP180 phosphosites (Ser600, Ser621 and Ser627) are dephosphorylated, one of which (Ser627) is located in the reported binding site.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Phosphorylation of dynamin1 by PKC at Ser795 prevents its association with phospholipids.
source: For instance, phosphorylation of dynamin1 by PKC at Ser795 prevents its association with phospholipids (Powell et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Powell et al., 2000.

claim: Downregulation of synapsin1 Ser62 was observed upon stimulation.
source: For synapsin1, regulation of some of the sites has been previously characterized extensively (Jovanovic et al., 2001). Such as downregulation of Ser62 and upregulation of Ser556 and Ser603.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to prior characterization by Jovanovic et al., 2001.

claim: Upregulation of synapsin1 Ser556 and Ser603 was observed upon stimulation.
source: For synapsin1, regulation of some of the sites has been previously characterized extensively (Jovanovic et al., 2001). Such as downregulation of Ser62 and upregulation of Ser556 and Ser603.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to prior characterization by Jovanovic et al., 2001.

claim: No stimulus-dependent changes were observable at the phosphorylation sites of CdK5 (Ser549 and 551) in synapsin1.
source: However, no stimulus-dependent changes were observable at the phosphorylation sites of CdK5 (Ser549 and 551) that were suggested to regulate the size of the synaptic vesicle pools (Verstegen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to prior work by Verstegen et al., 2014.

claim: 48 phosphosites on bassoon were quantified in the experiments.
source: Our results show that, the proteins bassoon and piccolo are massively phosphorylated, with 48 and 31 sites being quantified in our experiments, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: 31 phosphosites on piccolo were quantified in the experiments.
source: Our results show that, the proteins bassoon and piccolo are massively phosphorylated, with 48 and 31 sites being quantified in our experiments, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Most of the piccolo phosphosites remained unchanged following stimulation, with the exception of 6 phosphosites.
source: Intriguingly, with the exception of 6 phosphosites, most of the piccolo phosphosites remained unchanged following stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Bassoon exhibited a dramatic decrease in phosphorylation at multiple sites in addition to increased phosphorylation at 5 other positions.
source: In comparison, bassoon exhibited a dramatic decrease in phosphorylation at multiple sites in addition to increased phosphorylation at 5 other positions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Bassoon and piccolo have different protein interaction partners despite having similar structural motifs.
source: In previous studies it has been reported that in spite of having similar structural motifs, bassoon and piccolo have different protein interaction partners (Takao-Rikitsu et al., 2004; Schoch and Gundelfinger, 2006; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takao-Rikitsu et al., 2004; Schoch and Gundelfinger, 2006; Wang et al., 2009.

claim: The more pronounced dephosphorylation of phosphosites in bassoon compared to piccolo can explain their different protein interactions.
source: The more pronounced observed dephosphorylation of phosphosites in bassoon compared to piccolo can be an explanation for their different protein interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: 7 regulated phosphosites were identified on RIM that are distributed along the protein.
source: Here, we identified 7 regulated phosphosites that are distributed along the protein (Figure 5) including Ser413 that was previously reported to be phosphorylated by PKA, and its role in presynaptic long-term plasticity has been discussed extensively (Lonart et al., 2003; Kaeser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: RIM Ser413 was previously reported to be phosphorylated by PKA, and its role in presynaptic long-term plasticity has been discussed extensively.
source: Here, we identified 7 regulated phosphosites that are distributed along the protein (Figure 5) including Ser413 that was previously reported to be phosphorylated by PKA, and its role in presynaptic long-term plasticity has been discussed extensively (Lonart et al., 2003; Kaeser et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lonart et al., 2003 and Kaeser et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphosites upregulated during Ca2+-dependent stimulation were highly enriched for the RxxS sequence motif.
source: Phosphosites upregulated during Ca2+-dependent stimulation were highly enriched for the RxxS sequence motif (7.36 fold, p=1.0 × 10–16 compared to control and 5.98 fold, p=4.8 × 10–13, when compared to samples depolarized in the absence of Ca2+)(Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the Motif-X analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: RxxS is the consensus motif of calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) but also targeted by protein kinase A (PKA) and conventional isoforms of protein kinase C (PKC).
source: RxxS is the consensus motif of calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) but also targeted by protein kinase A (PKA) and conventional isoforms of protein kinase C (PKC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinase consensus motifs.

claim: CaMKII, PKA, and PKC are activated upon depolarization of nerve terminals in the presence of Ca2+ ions.
source: This is in agreement with previous studies showing that these kinases are activated upon depolarization of nerve terminals in the presence of Ca2+ ions (Millán et al., 2003; Yamauchi, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Millán et al., 2003 and Yamauchi, 2005.

claim: The SP motif is preferred by proline-directed kinases such as ERK1/2, GSK-3 and Cdk5.
source: However, the SP motif is preferred by proline-directed kinases such as ERK1/2, GSK-3 and Cdk5 (Guan et al., 1991; Lee et al., 1997; Veeranna et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guan et al., 1991; Lee et al., 1997; Veeranna et al., 1998.

claim: The study quantified upregulation of two activating phosphosites in the active loop of ERK1/2 (T183, Y185).
source: Between the mentioned kinases, ERK1/2 is less likely to be inactivated upon stimulation, since we have quantified the upregulation of two activating phosphosites in the active loop of ERK1/2 (T183, Y185, Supplementary file 2, K+, EGTA vs K+, Ca2+).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The balance between the activation of calcineurin (PP2B) and Cdk5 controls the dynamics of resting and recycling pools as well as activity of voltage gated calcium channels.
source: The balance between the activation of calcineurin (PP2B) and Cdk5 is reported to control the dynamics of resting and recycling pools as well as activity of voltage gated calcium channels (Kim and Ryan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Ryan, 2013.

claim: Cdk5 and GSK-3 phosphorylate P/Q- and N-type voltage-dependent calcium channels.
source: For example, Cdk5 and GSK-3 phosphorylate P/Q- and N-type voltage-dependent calcium channels (Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010) whereas ERK1/2 phosphorylate L-type calcium channels (Subramanian and Morozov, 2011) and phosphorylation decreases the activity of both types of calcium channels.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010; Subramanian and Morozov, 2011.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylate L-type calcium channels.
source: For example, Cdk5 and GSK-3 phosphorylate P/Q- and N-type voltage-dependent calcium channels (Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010) whereas ERK1/2 phosphorylate L-type calcium channels (Subramanian and Morozov, 2011) and phosphorylation decreases the activity of both types of calcium channels.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010; Subramanian and Morozov, 2011.

claim: Phosphorylation decreases the activity of P/Q-, N-type, and L-type calcium channels.
source: For example, Cdk5 and GSK-3 phosphorylate P/Q- and N-type voltage-dependent calcium channels (Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010) whereas ERK1/2 phosphorylate L-type calcium channels (Subramanian and Morozov, 2011) and phosphorylation decreases the activity of both types of calcium channels.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tomizawa et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2010; Subramanian and Morozov, 2011.

claim: The increase in Ca2+ concentration activates phosphatase PP2B (calcineurin).
source: However, the increase in the Ca2+ concentration activates phosphatase PP2B (calcineurin) (Sun et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation changes in Neurabin-2 (S100), regulatory protein of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1), were observed upon stimulation.
source: We also observe phosphorylation changes in Neurabin-2 (S100), regulatory protein of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1), (Supplementary file 2, K+, EGTA vs K+, Ca2+).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Phosphorylation of S100 in Neurabin-2 alters PP1 localization by decreasing binding affinity to actin and causing diffusion from the nerve terminal.
source: It has been shown previously that phosphorylation of S100 alters PP1 localization by the decrease of binding affinity to actin and the diffusion from the nerve terminal (Colbran, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colbran, 2004.

claim: Upon Ca2+ influx, PKA, PKC, CaMKII, PP2A and PP2B are activated.
source: In summary, our data suggest that upon Ca2+ influx subset of kinases and phosphatases such as PKA, PKC, CaMKII, PP2A and PP2B are activated while PP1 is less active and the target sites of proline directed kinases show a decrease in phosphorylation, mediated either by decreased activity of the kinases or preferred targeting by the phosphatases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and motif analysis.

claim: Upon Ca2+ influx, PP1 is less active.
source: In summary, our data suggest that upon Ca2+ influx subset of kinases and phosphatases such as PKA, PKC, CaMKII, PP2A and PP2B are activated while PP1 is less active and the target sites of proline directed kinases show a decrease in phosphorylation, mediated either by decreased activity of the kinases or preferred targeting by the phosphatases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and motif analysis.

claim: Upon Ca2+ influx, the target sites of proline directed kinases show a decrease in phosphorylation.
source: In summary, our data suggest that upon Ca2+ influx subset of kinases and phosphatases such as PKA, PKC, CaMKII, PP2A and PP2B are activated while PP1 is less active and the target sites of proline directed kinases show a decrease in phosphorylation, mediated either by decreased activity of the kinases or preferred targeting by the phosphatases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and motif analysis.

claim: RIM1 Ser413 was phosphorylated only by PKA in the in vitro kinase assay.
source: For instance, RIM1 Ser413 was phosphorylated only by PKA; consistent with a previous report (Lonart et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro kinase assay, with reference to prior work by Lonart et al., 2003.

claim: RIM1 Ser1141 was phosphorylated mostly by CaMKII and with lower efficiency by PKA.
source: RIM1 Ser1141 was phosphorylated mostly by CaMKII and with lower efficiency by PKA.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Bassoon Ser2844 was phosphorylated only by CaMKII.
source: Bassoon Ser2844 was phosphorylated only by CaMKII.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Piccolo Ser3626 was phosphorylated by CaMKII and PKA albeit with low efficiency.
source: Piccolo Ser3626 was phosphorylated by CaMKII and PKA albeit with low efficiency.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Liprin-α3 Ser75 was phosphorylated by all three kinases (CaMKII, PKA, PKC) although PKC was less efficient.
source: Liprin-α3 Ser75 was the only phosphosite that was phosphorylated by all three kinases although PKC was less efficient.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Synaptosomes retain the ability to synthesize ATP, maintain the resting potential and respond to depolarization with Ca2+-influx and Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: Synaptosomes retain the ability to synthesize ATP, maintain the resting potential and respond to depolarization with Ca2+-influx and Ca2+-dependent exocytosis of synaptic vesicles (Nicholls, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholls, 2003.

claim: Synaptosomes respond to external signals and to activators and inhibitors of various steps of the synaptic vesicle cycle.
source: Synaptosomes respond not only to external signals but also to activators and inhibitors of various steps of the synaptic vesicle cycle such as clostridial neurotoxins (Blasi et al., 1994), black widow spider venom (Nicholls et al., 1982), or dynamin inhibitors such as dynasore (Daniel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blasi et al., 1994; Nicholls et al., 1982; Daniel et al., 2012.

claim: The phosphorylation changes observed after stimulation are dominated by Ca2+-dependent kinases and phosphatases.
source: This agrees well with the observation that depolarization in the absence of Ca2+ resulted only in very limited changes of the phosphosite pattern. This is remarkable when considering that clamp-depolarization by potassium is nonphysiological and may have deleterious side effects (e.g. drop in ATP levels). Consequently, our data show that the phosphorylation changes observed after stimulation are dominated by Ca2+-dependent kinases (such as CaMKII, PKC) and phosphatases (such as calcineurin), all of which are implicated in regulating presynaptic function (Scholz and Palfrey, 1998; Brager et al., 2003; Leenders and Sheng, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with references to Scholz and Palfrey, 1998; Brager et al., 2003; Leenders and Sheng, 2005.

claim: Calcineurin upregulates adenylate cyclase in nerve terminals, increasing cAMP levels and activating protein kinase A.
source: For instance, calcineurin upregulates adenylate cyclase in nerve terminals (Ferguson and Storm, 2004; Chan et al., 2005), increasing cAMP levels and activating protein kinase A.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferguson and Storm, 2004 and Chan et al., 2005.

claim: The data suggest that CdK5, ERK1/2 and GSK-3 are downregulated upon stimulation.
source: Moreover, our motif enrichment analysis suggests that CdK5, ERK1/2 and GSK-3 are downregulated upon stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motif enrichment analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The activity of kinases and phosphatases is precisely coordinated upon Ca2+ entry.
source: We conclude that the activity of kinases and phosphatases is precisely coordinated: upon Ca2+ entry, CaMKII, PKA, PKC as well as PP2A and PP2B are activated whereas proline directed kinases (e.g. CdK5 and GSK-3) as well as PP1 appear to be downregulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and motif analysis.

claim: The panoply of phosphorylation sites and phosphorylation changes detected in many proteins of the presynaptic active zone was surprising.
source: The panoply of phosphorylation sites and phosphorylation changes detected in many proteins of the presynaptic active zone was surprising.
evidence: This is a subjective assessment of the findings by the authors.

claim: Phosphorylation dependent binding of 14-3-3 adaptor protein to bassoon at Ser2844 has been previously studied.
source: Only a few of these phosphorylation sites have been previously studied, such as phosphorylation dependent binding of 14-3-3 adaptor protein to bassoon at Ser2844 or the cAMP-regulated site in RIM1 (Ser413) that plays a role in long-term potentiation (Lonart et al., 2003; Kaeser et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lonart et al., 2003 and Kaeser et al., 2008.

claim: The cAMP-regulated site in RIM1 (Ser413) plays a role in long-term potentiation.
source: Only a few of these phosphorylation sites have been previously studied, such as phosphorylation dependent binding of 14-3-3 adaptor protein to bassoon at Ser2844 or the cAMP-regulated site in RIM1 (Ser413) that plays a role in long-term potentiation (Lonart et al., 2003; Kaeser et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lonart et al., 2003 and Kaeser et al., 2008.

claim: Multi-site phosphorylation may modulate the binding affinity of a protein to other proteins or block binding by increasing its overall negative charge.
source: Multi-site phosphorylation may modulate the binding affinity of a protein to other proteins or block binding by increasing its overall negative charge leading to repulsion from other proteins and charged membrane lipids (Powell et al., 2000; Arbuzova et al., 2002; Ferreon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell et al., 2000; Arbuzova et al., 2002; Ferreon et al., 2009.

claim: The data only represent a snapshot of phosphorylation changes 2 min after depolarization.
source: Also, our data only represent a snapshot of phosphorylation changes 2 min after depolarization, i.e. when exo- and endocytosis are both at elevated steady-state levels.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its limitations.

claim: Transient changes occurring in the first seconds after stimulation may have been missed.
source: Thus it is conceivable that transient changes occurring in the first seconds after stimulations were missed.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: No significant changes were observed in the phosphorylation status of SNARE and other proteins mediating exocytosis of synaptic vesicles.
source: Intriguingly, in our data no significant changes were observed in the phosphorylation status of SNARE and other proteins that are mediating exocytosis of synaptic vesicles (e.g syntaxin1A Thr10, Ser14 (Rickman and Duncan, 2010), Ser59, Ser64; VAMP-2 Ser75, Ser80; SNAP-25 Ser25; Munc18 Ser506, Ser507, Ser509, Ser593 and NSF Ser739) (Supplementary file 2, Kohansal-Nodehi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The rapid feedback loops governed by kinases and phosphatases activated during stimulation do not target the exocytotic machinery itself but rather upstream processes such as docking, priming, and endocytosis.
source: Thus it appears that the rapid feedback loops governed by kinases and phosphatases, which are activated during stimulation, do not target the exocytotic machinery itself but rather upstream processes such as docking, priming, and endocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Synaptosomes are uniquely suitable for the study of phosphorylation-dephosphorylation events associated with synaptic vesicle cycling.
source: Synaptosomes are uniquely suitable for the study of phosphorylation-dephosphorylation events that are associated with synaptic vesicle cycling.
evidence: This is a statement about the suitability of the experimental system.

claim: Synaptosomes represent the only compartment in the extract that forms membrane enclosed structures retaining basic cellular properties.
source: Although even the most highly enriched fraction of nerve terminals still contains significant contamination from many other parts of the starting tissue (as confirmed by the composition of the proteome of this fraction), synaptosomes represent the only compartment in the extract that forms membrane enclosed structures retaining basic cellular properties.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of synaptosomes based on established knowledge.

claim: Physiological ATP-levels can only be maintained inside nerve terminals whereas residual external ATP is likely to be rapidly degraded by ATPases.
source: Thus, physiological ATP-levels can only be maintained inside nerve terminals whereas residual external ATP is likely to be rapidly degraded by ATPases, in particular by uncoupled ion pumps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of synaptosomes and cellular biochemistry.

claim: Protein kinases can only operate inside the nerve terminal during the experiment.
source: Consequently, protein kinases can only operate inside the nerve terminal during the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATP requirements of kinases and the properties of synaptosomes.

claim: An almost identical pattern of regulated sites was observed regardless of whether the Ca2+-free control was depolarized or not.
source: Second, almost an identical pattern of regulated sites was observed regardless of whether the Ca2+-free control was depolarized or not.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of the experimental data.
